title: MA8-13628
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal female claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, and her spouse, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, are citizens of Israel and were originally from the former USSR. The claimants allege that they are "Convention refugees" and "persons in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimants are Jews who were born in the USSR. They left the USSR in 1990, before the fall of the Soviet regime in 1991. They were Russian citizens at the time.
The principal female claimant alleges that she was subjected to anti-Semitic attacks and that she and her family sought refuge in Israel.
When they arrived in that country, they met an Arab family, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, in 1991. This family drove them to a bomb shelter in XXXXX 1991 and continued to help them afterward.

After the start of the Intifada of 2000, XXXXX was attacked by some Israelis. The female claimant tried to protect him, but she was threatened. When the female claimant XXXXX was pushed, her husband and her son-in-law came out to protect her.

The female claimant alleged that she was insulted repeatedly by the neighbours who called the police whenever XXXXX and his family came to visit. During the war with Lebanon in 2006, hostility against the Arabs increased even more.

On XXXXX, 2007, the female claimant and her family went to the suburbs with the family of their friend XXXXX. While the men were playing volleyball, they noticed one of their neighbours going towards Mr. XXXXX and pushing him roughly. The latter fell to the ground and XXXXX tried to help him but a large number of men then started to hit him.
XXXXX had to be taken to the hospital while his spouse went to a police station. She stated that they did not receive any help whatsoever.

They telephoned their daughter XXXXX who lives in Montréal and decided to claim refugee protection in that country. They entered the country on XXXXX, 2007, and claimed refugee protection on June 4 of the same year.
After analyzing the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel determines that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection".

Considering the documents submitted as evidence, namely the photocopies of the claimants' Israeli passports, which are valid from XXXXX, 2003, to XXXXX, 2013, their American visas issued on XXXXX, 2007, which are valid for ten years, their birth certificates issued on XXXXX, 1944, for the female claimant, and on XXXXX, 1980 for the male claimant, the panel is satisfied as to the claimants' identities.
The panel is of the opinion that the abuse alleged by the claimants is more in keeping with harassment and is not serious enough to be considered persecution.

In fact, during their stay in Israel, the claimants were undoubtedly subjected to harassment from the Jewish society because they were not Jewish. The incidents that they fear should they return consist of condescending treatment towards them by the population in general because of their Russian origin and their Christianity. They also fear the attitude of some police officers when they conduct identity checks.

The female claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, mentioned a few incidents that took place with the neighbours and relates that, among other incidents, the neighbours left garbage, including dog hair and other junk on their doorstep. She also added that the neighbours harassed them by continually telephoning the police. However, when she was questioned about this, she stated that this happened three times and that the police simply checked their papers and did not add anything else.

The claimant XXXXX XXXXX stated that a neighbour pushed him once in a park, when he was with an Arabic family who were friends of his, and he sprained his wrist. The panel is of the opinion that these acts are definitely unpleasant, but that they do not qualify as serious abuse.

The panel is of the opinion that the treatment described by the claimants, which they fear will recur should they return to Israel, does not qualify as persecution, as the concept has been developed through jurisprudence. In fact, in order to consider actual or anticipated mistreatment as persecution, it must constitute serious hardship. To determine the severity of an anticipated prejudice, the panel must analyze whether the incidents feared by the claimants constitute an infringement on fundamental rights, as much in the existence of these rights, as in their enjoyment, their expression or their exercise.1 This analysis was supported by the Supreme Court in Ward,2 where the following definition is given for persecution: "sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection". The claimants have not proven that one or more of their fundamental rights had been violated.

The treatment that the claimants fear is not of a degree that could lead to the conclusion that their fear of persecution is well-founded, even though their lives in Israel might have been difficult at times. However, the panel is of the opinion that the treatment experienced by the claimants in Israel, and that they fear should they return-even considering the cumulative effect of the actions taken against them-does not constitute persecution.
Among other things, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants did not make use of the recourse that was available to them in their country before coming to Canada to claim refugee protection.

The panel wanted to know whether the claimants had filed a complaint regarding their alleged problems. The female claimant stated that when her husband was taken to the hospital, she and her son-in-law went to file a complaint in the city where they were for their outing of XXXXX, 2007. However, given that no document on that subject has been submitted, the panel enquired as to what happened when the female claimant went to the police. The female claimant's testimony was vague and did not contain much detail. The panel had to question her on every stage of her undertaking, and she eventually mentioned, although only in reply to questions by the panel, that the police took notes and that they asked for her name and address. When asked whether she had requested a copy of her complaint, she stated that she did not think of it because she was worried about her husband. The panel understands these concerns but, considering that the female claimant thought of going to the police while someone else drove her husband to the hospital, it was feasible that she could have thought of requesting a copy of her complaint, given that she took the time to go file the complaint; however, this was not the case. When asked whether she had thought of requesting a copy of her complaint after she arrived in Canada, she replied that she had not because she did not know how to proceed. The panel does not believe that the female claimant filed a complaint, since she is at pains to explain how she did so and she did not submit any corroborating document, even though she entered Canada on XXXXX, 2007, almost three years ago, which would have given her adequate time to do so.

When asked whether she had contacted any other organization to file a complaint, she stated that she consulted a lawyer, but she had difficulty in giving his name. She eventually stated that it was XXXXX XXXXX. When asked what he had allegedly done, she stated that he did nothing, that he simply said that it was not worth the trouble. The panel is of the opinion that if the claimants had consulted a lawyer, it is plausible that he would have offered more support or at least told them about the ombudsman, which does not appear to have been the case. The panel does not believe that this consultation took place.

The panel questioned the female claimant about the ombudsman, and mentioned that the organization was founded in 1971 and that it is there to help citizens. The document filed under Tab 13.1) clearly states that: [Translation] ...Office of the Ombudsman was created in order to "examine complaints from every stratum of society," particularly from more vulnerable groups such as new immigrants... Other organizations, such as the Association for Civil Rights in Israel and Israel's Ministry of Immigrant Absorption offer a number of services to settle newly arrived immigrants in many languages.3

However, the female claimant replied that she is not familiar with that organization and that she has no idea what it is about. The panel is of the opinion that the claimants did not file a complaint about the alleged threats; prior to claiming refugee protection in Canada, the female claimant and her husband were required to exhaust all the recourse offered by their country and they neglected to do so.

Given that the claimants did not use the resources that were available in Israel before leaving, and that the panel is of the opinion that the claimants' problems do not constitute persecution, the panel is of the opinion that the evidence submitted by the claimants is insufficient to establish a fear of returning to their country and a risk to their life.

After analyzing all the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimants did not demonstrate that there is a "serious possibility" that they would be persecuted under one of the Convention grounds, that is to say, imputed political opinion or membership in a particular social group, the elderly, if they were to return to their country, Israel. They also did not demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that, should they return to Israel, they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

Their claims for refugee protection are rejected.
